`pg_parquet` is a PostgreSQL extension that allows you to read and write Parquet files, which are located in `S3`, `Azure Blob Storage`, `Google Cloud Storage`, `http(s) endpoints` or `file system`, from PostgreSQL via `COPY TO/FROM` commands. It depends on Apache Arrow project to read and write Parquet files and pgrx project to extend PostgreSQL's `COPY` command.
> A `map` column requires the crunchy_map extension. The command

The `stats_geospatial` column reports the bounding box and the geometry types that Parquet computed for a geospatial column, as `jsonb`. It is `NULL` for the columns that have no geospatial statistics, which are all of the columns except the `geometry` and `geography` ones. The geometry types are the ISO WKB codes that the Parquet geospatial specification lists, e.g. `1` is a point and `2` is a linestring. The `zmin`, `zmax`, `mmin` and `mmax` bounds are only reported for the geometries that have those dimensions. A PostGIS type that the Parquet geospatial specification does not cover, e.g. a curved, triangulated or polyhedral one, is refused rather than written, as described below. A `geography` column always reports its geometry types, but its bounding box is only reported when all of its geometries are points: the edges of a `geography` are geodesics, which can reach beyond the box that the coordinates of their endpoints give.
The progress of an ongoing `COPY TO/FROM` a Parquet file is reported to the pg_stat_progress_copy view.

The credentials of an object store are read from the environment of the postgres process, as described below for each store, and never from the uri: a uri that carries credentials before its host is rejected rather than signed with the credentials of the environment while its own are only written into the logs. A session can make its requests with credentials of its own instead, by naming a profile that the administrator mapped to its role, which is described under Session Profiles, or by putting them in parameters of its own where the server allows that, which is described under Credentials In Parameters.
- `AWS_<HTTP CLIENT OPTION>`: an http client option, e.g. `AWS_TIMEOUT` **(only via environment variables)**
The simplest way to configure object storage is by creating the standard `~/.azure/config` file:
- `AZURE_CONFIG_DIRECTORY`: the directory the config files of the session profiles are kept in **(only via environment variables)**
- `AZURE_<HTTP CLIENT OPTION>`: an http client option, e.g. `AZURE_TIMEOUT` **(only via environment variables)**
- `HTTP_<HTTP CLIENT OPTION>`: an http client option, e.g. `HTTP_TIMEOUT` **(only via environment variables)**
- `GOOGLE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_DIRECTORY`: the directory the service account keys of the session profiles are kept in **(only via environment variables)**
- `GOOGLE_<HTTP CLIENT OPTION>`: an http client option, e.g. `GOOGLE_TIMEOUT` **(only via environment variables)**

They are read **ahead of** a profile and of the environment both: a session that set `pg_parquet.aws_access_key_id` makes its `s3://` requests with what it set, whichever profile it named, and a credential that does not work fails the copy rather than falling back to the credentials of the server. Setting `pg_parquet.allow_credentials_in_parameters` back to `off` stops them being read at once, including in a session that already set them. A store built from them is not cached, so replacing a parameter replaces the identity the next copy is made with.

> The last of those hides a credential, it does not keep it: `SHOW pg_parquet.aws_secret_access_key` and `current_setting('pg_parquet.aws_secret_access_key')` read it in full, from any session that set it. Nothing here makes a credential in a parameter safe from the log — only the places it is refused from are closed. A deployment that cannot have credentials in its log should leave this off and name a profile instead.

PostGIS has geometry types that the Parquet geospatial specification does not define: the curved ones (`CIRCULARSTRING`, `COMPOUNDCURVE`, `CURVEPOLYGON`, `MULTICURVE`, `MULTISURFACE`), and `TIN`, `POLYHEDRALSURFACE` and `TRIANGLE`. Their WKB type codes are `8`, `9`, `10`, `11`, `12`, `16`, `15` and `17`, where the specification defines `1` to `7` and the same codes plus 1000 per extra dimension.

- `pg_parquet.profile_name`: the profile the session's object store credentials are read from, as described under Session Profiles. The default is unset, which reads the credentials of the server's environment. Any role may set it, and `parquet.user_profile_mapping` is what says which profiles a role may name.

- `pg_parquet.allow_credentials_in_parameters`: you can set this parameter to `on` to let a session put the credentials of an object store into parameters of its own, as described under Credentials In Parameters. The default is `off`, and only a superuser may change it, since a credential set that way is written into the server log and read from `pg_stat_activity`. The credential parameters themselves are refused while this is off.

- For `COPY TO`, each worker writes a range of the table's pages, and the ranges end up in the destination without being re-encoded. For an `s3://`, `az://` or `gs://` destination, every worker uploads the ranges it wrote as parts of the destination's own multipart upload and the backend only adds the file's footer, so each byte of the file is uploaded once, nothing is downloaded, and nothing of such a copy is written to local disk. A copy whose server crashes can leave an unfinished multipart upload behind, which the bucket's own rule for incomplete uploads is what removes. A part that is left behind this way holds the rows of the copy that wrote it, so a uri pattern that covers it skips it rather than reading those rows again, and reports it as a file the pattern does not read. The parts of that upload differ in size, which a store that requires all but the last part to be the same size, e.g. Cloudflare R2, rejects. The bytes of a range are uploaded as the range wrote them, header and footer included, so the destination holds a little under 1% of bytes nothing points at. For a local file, each worker writes a part file next to the destination instead, and the backend merges the parts into it. With `file_size_bytes` the destination is a folder of complete files, so each worker writes files of its own into it rather than parts of one file, and the file a worker is in the middle of is finished before its range ends, which leaves a few more and smaller files behind than a single process copy writes. The files of such a folder are numbered in the order the workers claim them, so the rows of the table are not in the order of the file names. Parallel `COPY TO` applies to a single non-temporary heap table copied to a plain local file, to a folder of files, or to one of those object stores; anything else, e.g. `COPY (SELECT ..) TO`, a `COPY TO PROGRAM` or `TO STDOUT`, or an `http://` uri, is copied by a single process. Note that each range writes its own row groups, so a parallel `COPY TO` ends up with more and smaller row groups than a single process one.

- For `COPY FROM`, each worker decodes a subset of the row groups of the file and hands the rows to the backend that runs the command, which is the only one that writes them into the relation, in the order the file holds them. A uri with a wildcard stands for several files, whose row groups are one list the workers split between themselves the same way, each worker opening the file its next row group is in. Parallel `COPY FROM` applies to files, local, on an `s3://`, `az://` or `gs://` store, or at an `http(s)` endpoint that serves byte ranges, holding more than one row group together, read into a non-temporary heap table that has no row triggers and no attribute the command leaves to a default, an identity or a generation expression; anything else, e.g. a `COPY FROM PROGRAM`, is copied by a single process. Because only one process may write into the relation, the speedup is bounded by how fast that one process can insert, which the decoding of a few workers is usually enough to reach.
> * `numeric(P <= 9, S)` is represented as `INT32` with `DECIMAL` logical type
> * `numeric(9 < P <= 18, S)` is represented as `INT64` with `DECIMAL` logical type
> * `numeric(18 < P <= 38, S)` is represented as `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY(9-16)` with `DECIMAL` logical type
> * `numeric(38 < P, S)` is represented as `BYTE_ARRAY` with `STRING` logical type

> * `numeric` is allowed by Postgres. (precision and scale not specified). These are represented by a default precision (38) and scale (9) instead of writing them as string. You get runtime error if your table tries to write a numeric value which is not allowed by the default precision and scale (29 integral digits before decimal point, 9 digits after decimal point). Reading into such a column keeps all the digits of the file's value, be it a decimal or a string, since Postgres stores an unbounded numeric at any precision and scale.

> - (4) The `geometry` and `geography` types are represented as `BYTE_ARRAY` encoded as `WKB` with the `GEOMETRY` and `GEOGRAPHY` logical types, specified by the parquet geospatial spec, when `postgis` extension is created. Otherwise, they are represented as `BYTE_ARRAY` with `STRING` logical type. The `crs` of the logical type is taken from the `srid` of the column's type modifier, e.g. `geometry(point, 3857)` is written with the `EPSG:3857` crs. A column whose `srid` is lon/lat on the `WGS84` ellipsoid is written with the default crs of the spec, which is `OGC:CRS84`, and a `geometry` column without an `srid` is written with the unset crs of the spec, which is `srid:0`. An `srid` that no authority in `spatial_ref_sys` claims is written with the engine specific `srid:<code>` form of the spec, e.g. `srid:990000`, so that it is not mistaken for an unset crs. An `srid` whose `auth_name` holds the `:` separator, or is `srid` itself, takes that same form, since its `authority:code` form would not read back as this `srid`. A `geography` column without an `srid` is written with the default crs, since PostGIS geographies are on the `WGS84` ellipsoid. The bounding box and the geometry types of each column are written as geospatial statistics, except for the bounding box of a `geography` column that has edges, as described above. A geometry whose type the specification does not cover is refused rather than written, as described above. On read, the `srid` of the geometries is restored from the `crs` of the logical type, resolving its `authority:code` form through `spatial_ref_sys` and taking the code of its `srid:<code>` form as the `srid` itself, and falls back to the `srid` of the target column's type modifier when the file has no `crs`.

> - (5) `crunchy_map` is dependent on functionality provided by Crunchy Bridge. The `crunchy_map` type is represented as `GROUP` with `MAP` logical type when `crunchy_map` extension is created. Otherwise, it is represented as `BYTE_ARRAY` with `STRING` logical type.

Recipy stores all of its configuration and the database itself in `~/.recipy`. Recipy's main configuration file is inside this folder, called `recipyrc`. The configuration file format is very simple, and is based on Windows INI files - and having a configuration file is completely optional: the defaults will work fine with no configuration file.
* `editor = vi` - Configure the default text editor that will be used when recipy needs you to type in a message. Use notepad if on Windows, for example
* `port` - specify port to use for the GUI
* `file_diff_outputs` - store diff between the old output and new output file, if the output file exists before the script is executed
* `path = /path/to/file.json` - set the path to the database file
* `diff` - don't store the output of `git diff` in the metadata for a recipy run
* `git` - don't store anything relating to git (origin, commit, repo etc) in the metadata for a recipy run
* `input_hashes` - don't compute and store SHA-1 hashes of input files
* `output_hashes` - don't compute and store SHA-1 hashes of output files
* List any module here (eg. `numpy`) to instruct recipy *not* to record inputs from this module, or `all` to ignore inputs from all modules
* List any module here (eg. `numpy`) to instruct recipy *not* to record outputs from this module, or `all` to ignore outputs from all modules

- Description: Faiss is a library developed by Facebook AI Research that provides efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors. It is designed for use with large-scale, high-dimensional data and supports several index types and algorithms for various use cases.
- Indexing methods: LSH, PQ, HNSW, and more
- Installation and usage: Faiss can be installed using pip or conda, and its API is well-documented with examples available in the official repository.

- Description: Annoy (Approximate Nearest Neighbors Oh Yeah) is a C++ library created by Spotify for approximate nearest neighbor search. It is memory-efficient and optimized for fast query times. Annoy is particularly useful when dealing with large datasets, and it supports static and dynamic datasets.
- Memory-mapped files for sharing indices between processes
- Custom distance metrics: Euclidean, Manhattan, Angular, and more
- Python, C++, and other language bindings
- Installation and usage: Annoy can be installed using pip, and it has an easy-to-use Python API with examples and tutorials available on the project's GitHub page.

- Description: Milvus is an open-source vector database built for AI and analytics applications. It supports multiple index types and provides powerful scalability and performance. Milvus is designed for managing massive high-dimensional data and enables efficient similarity search and analytics.
- Indexing methods: IVF, HNSW, PQ, and more
- Hybrid search: combining scalar and vector filtering
- RESTful API and Python, Java, Node.js, and C++ SDKs
- Installation and usage: Milvus can be installed using Docker or built from source, and it comes with extensive documentation and examples to help you get started.

- Description: HNSWLIB is an open-source C++ library for approximate nearest neighbor search, which implements the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) algorithm. It is designed for high-performance similarity search in large-scale datasets with various distance metrics.
- Custom distance metrics: Euclidean, Cosine, L1, and more
- Installation and usage: HNSWLIB can be installed using pip, and its API is easy to use with Python and C++ examples provided in the official repository.

- Description: Non-Metric Space Library (NMSLIB) is an open-source, highly efficient library for similarity search and nearest neighbor search in generic metric and non-metric spaces. It supports various similarity search algorithms and distance functions, making it suitable for a wide range of applications.
- Indexing methods: HNSW, SW-graph, VPTree, and more
- Custom distance metrics: Euclidean, Cosine, Jaccard, and more
- Efficient index construction and query processing
- Installation and usage: NMSLIB can be installed using pip or built from source, and it offers a Python API with examples and documentation available on the project's GitHub page.

- Description: Cottontail DB is a column store aimed at multimedia retrieval. It allows for classical boolean as well as vector-space retrieval (nearest neighbour search) used in similarity search using a unified data and query model.
- Indexing methods: VAF, PQ, LSH, and more
- gRPC interface with per-built clients for Java/Kotlin and Python

- Description: Vexvault is a document storage system which is 100% browser based. Vexvault is designed to make your files and data accessible to AI applications like ChatGPT, all while ensuring the users privacy and security. It tries to be as easy to integrate and use as possible.
- scalability by pushing embedding calculation to the edge
- fast, because it can omit the network
- large amount of storage through use of indexedb

- Description: Pinecone is a managed vector database designed for large-scale machine learning applications. It provides a simple API for creating and managing vector indices, enabling fast and accurate similarity search across billions of items.
- Indexing methods: HNSW, PQ, and more
- Integration with popular machine learning frameworks
- Pricing and usage: Pinecone offers a free tier with limited resources, as well as pay-as-you-go and enterprise plans with additional features and support.

- Description: Vespa is a real-time, scalable search, recommendation, and analytics engine developed by Yahoo. It supports efficient similarity search on high-dimensional vectors and allows for complex queries combining structured and unstructured data.
- Indexing methods: HNSW, ANN, and more
- Support for structured data and text search
- RESTful API and Java, Python, and Node.js clients

- Pricing and usage: Vespa is available as a managed service on the Vespa Cloud platform, with pricing based on resource consumption and data storage. A self-hosted option is also available for on-premises or cloud deployment.

- Description: Vector.ai is a managed vector search platform that provides an API for creating, managing, and searching vector indices. It is designed to handle large volumes of high-dimensional data, enabling efficient similarity search for machine learning and AI applications.
- Indexing methods: HNSW, PQ, and more
- Integration with popular machine learning frameworks
- Pricing and usage: Vector.ai offers a free tier with limited resources, as well as paid plans with additional features, support, and custom pricing for enterprise customers.

- Description: Qdrant is a high-performance vector search engine designed for efficient similarity search and management of large-scale, high-dimensional data. It offers a flexible API and a wide range of indexing methods, making it suitable for various use cases.
- Indexing methods: HNSW, IVF, and more
- RESTful API and Python, Java, Node.js, and C++ SDKs
- Pricing and usage: Qdrant offers a free trial with limited resources, as well as paid plans and custom enterprise pricing based on data storage and query volume.

- Description: Weaviate is an open-source, GraphQL-based vector search engine that enables similarity search on high-dimensional data. While it is open-source, the commercial version offers additional features, support, and managed services.
- Support for various data types: text, images, audio, and more
- Indexing methods: HNSW, ANN, and more

- Pricing and usage: Weaviate offers a free open-source version and a commercial version with additional features and managed services. Pricing for the commercial version depends on the resources needed and is available upon request.

- Description: NucliaDB is a versatile vector database designed for data scientists and machine learning experts working with HuggingFace and other data pipeline platforms. Built on top of the Tantivy library and written in Rust and Python, it is designed to efficiently index large datasets and provide multi-tenant support.
- Store text, files, vectors, labels, and annotations
- Integration with popular NLP pipelines (HuggingFace, PyTorch, etc)
- Indexing and storage of fields, paragraphs, and semantic sentences
- Support for multiple fields and metadata, including text, HTML, Markdown, and more
- Distributed storage layer support with TiKV and Redis
- PostgreSQL storage layer support for standalone installs
- Blob support with S3-compatible API, GCS, and PG drivers
- Replication of index storage and distributed search
